purpose: Bounded SIPP person-month bridge connecting adjacent SNAP status to child-care payment, assistance, and work-prevention constraints without treating participation as care adequacy or security.

events.geography: United States; 2025 SIPP public-use person-month slice, 2024 reference year
events.date_precision: November-to-December SNAP status pair with annual fall child-care fields; child-care fields are not December outcomes or notice dates
events.denominator: 2,295 no-SNAP and 351 SNAP stable-state person records for work-prevention comparison; paid-care and assistance universes differ; entry/exit child-care cells are sparse
events.method: Weighted descriptive SIPP comparison using official labels, 2025 public-use data, and Fay-BRR replicate weights; no program-effect estimate
events.missingness: No notice, application effort, benefit amount, care quality, exact monthly care timing, employer response, child outcome, trust, appeal, remedy, or later recovery is retained
events.exposure: Among stable-state records, paid child-care use was 31.0% for no-SNAP November-to-December records and 23.9% for SNAP records; receiving child-care assistance was 5.2% versus 14.6%; child-care arrangements prevented work or more work for 3.4% versus 7.4%
events.alternatives_before_action: Paid care, child-care assistance, family or informal care, nonwork, and work-with-care are possible routes, but the public comparison does not identify each person's feasible alternative or arrangement quality
events.immediate_burden_or_benefit: The SNAP stable-state group showed higher reported child-care assistance and work-prevention constraints despite lower paid-care use; this is compatible with different eligibility, need, employment, income, and household-composition mixes
events.choice_or_response: The same-person status comparison preserves SNAP stability and annual child-care fields; entry and exit cells are too sparse for a transition interpretation
events.person_or_actor_with_control: Households, care providers, employers, and SNAP rules shape the option set; the public-use comparison does not identify the notice, caseworker, provider, or household decision sequence
events.remedy_or_institutional_response: SNAP status and reported child-care assistance are observed, but no household-specific benefit adequacy, care remedy, appeal, or completed service is measured
events.immediate_outcome: Public-benefit status coexists with distinct paid-care, assistance, and work-prevention profiles
events.protected_outcome: Child-care assistance or paid care may protect work participation or household resources, but completion, reliability, and child wellbeing are not verified
events.sacrificed_outcome: Work opportunity, income, time, care quality, or household flexibility may be sacrificed; the comparison cannot assign the sacrifice to SNAP or care access
events.cost_risk_transfer: Care and benefit constraints may transfer risk between public systems, households, employers, and informal caregivers; the public layer does not identify who bears the remaining cost
events.later_outcome: Following-month housing/utility hardship is available in related SIPP transition layers, but this child-care bridge does not connect a person's care field to later work, earnings, child, health, trust, or recovery outcome
events.meaning_and_attribution: No event-linked fairness, blame, dignity, trust, or identity judgment is measured
events.public_or_collective_response: No appeal, complaint, organizing, political action, or later policy response is linked
events.counterexample: Continued SNAP receipt can coexist with work-prevention care constraints, and lower paid-care use can reflect assistance or limited ability to purchase care rather than lower need
events.source_and_uncertainty: SIPP 2025 public-use person-month slice with official labels and Fay-BRR replicate weights; stable-state comparison is descriptive, universes differ, and sparse entry/exit cells are not promoted

arrows.to: paid care, child-care assistance, or work-prevention constraint
arrows.evidence: The SIPP comparison uses the same identified person records for adjacent SNAP status and annual fall child-care fields
arrows.counterexample: The fields have different reference periods and universes; the comparison does not establish a SNAP effect
arrows.remaining_gap: Monthly care timing, need, eligibility, notice, and household sequence

arrows.evidence: The official SIPP field comparison reports work-prevention shares alongside paid-care and assistance shares
arrows.counterexample: Work prevention can reflect employment, household, health, income, or care conditions not caused by SNAP or assistance
arrows.remaining_gap: Employer response, hours, earnings, care quality, and feasible alternative

arrows.to: following material security or household stability
arrows.evidence: Related SIPP transition layers observe adjacent-month hardship, but this bridge does not join the care fields to that outcome for the same case
arrows.counterexample: Stable receipt can coexist with hardship, and the care fields are not a dated trigger or later outcome
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-person care-to-following hardship merge, benefit amount, food result, work/care trade-off, and design-based comparison

arrows.to: durable security, trust, action, or exit
arrows.evidence: The public SIPP bridge contains no episode-level remedy, trust, action, or later recovery endpoint
arrows.counterexample: Leaving a benefit or reducing paid care can reflect administrative change, improved resources, worsening need, or lack of alternatives
arrows.remaining_gap: Same-episode notice, adequacy, appeal, later care/work outcome, trust, action, and recovery

boundary: This ledger adds a same-person public-assistance and care-capacity bridge. It does not establish program impact, care adequacy, child wellbeing, benefit security, or durable recovery.
storage_boundary: No raw SIPP person-month or replicate files are retained; only bounded derived comparison fields and interpretation limits are represented.
